title: Israel Extends Arbitrary Detention of Leading Palestinian Doctor
content:

according to Israeli news outlet Haaretz

.




This is despite ongoing reports that Dr Abu Safiya, a leading voice in Gaza’s systematically decimated healthcare system, has been subjected to beatings and torture in Israeli detention. 




Lawyer Nasser Odeh 

reported in July

 that his client was barely recognisable since being transferred to Rakevet, a notorious underground wing of the Ramla prison complex in central Israel, where 

Palestinian prisoners are reportedly

 deprived of sunlight and subject to extreme violence. 




Odeh said Dr Abu Safiya was weak, on the verge of losing consciousness and bearing fresh bruises and torture marks on his head and body. He added that the doctor told him: “This is the last time you’ll see me… they brought me here to kill me.”

title: Man Charged With Destroying £45m US Warplane Using Axe and Ball Bearings
content:
An Irish man “effectively destroyed” a £45m ($60m) US military aircraft using an axe and ball bearings, prosecutors have alleged. 




Daithí Ó Corráin, 48, is accused of sneaking onto the tarmac at Shannon Airport in County Clare, Ireland, and barricading himself inside a US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules aircraft, before causing extensive damage to the plane. 




Ó Corráin allegedly cut wires and hydraulic lines, smashed every gauge in the cockpit, damaged the aircraft’s exterior with an axe, and poured ball bearings into its fuel tank. 




Prosecutors in New York have charged Ó Corráin, also known as David Curran, with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum prison sentence of ten years. 




Ó Corráin is alleged to have researched and planned the April 2026 attack for months 

according to court filings

 unsealed by prosecutors on Tuesday. 




“The damage inflicted rendered the aircraft inoperable,” the indictment states, “and based on the extent of the damage, the aircraft – worth approximately $60m – will not return to active flight status.” 




The aircraft was “en route to another country on US military assignment”, it adds.

title: Epstein ‘Did Not Die by Suicide and Was Strangled to Death’
content:

This contradicts the 

official ruling of death by suicide

 from New York City’s chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein’s autopsy, which was later supported by federal investigations. 




Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

Freeman is reportedly the first specialist to have had access to the examiner’s full records.

title: The Workers Who Made GTA 6 Are Voting on Whether to Form a Union
content:
UK-based workers at Rockstar Games are voting on whether to recognise a union in their workplace, as the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 is set to break records.




The ballot of around 1,600 workers runs from 12 to 26 November and could lead to the creation of the Rockstar Game Workers Union, which would be the biggest in the UK video games sector.




Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer at Rockstar, told Novara Media that game workers were being dragged into “a future of uncertainty”, and that the ballot was their chance to regain some control.




“As Rockstar workers we build games that set the industry standard. It’s time for us to build a workplace that does the same,” he said

.




The vote comes as the games giant faces an employment tribunal over the dismissal of dozens of workers.




Rockstar sacked 31 UK-based union members without warning in October 2025, in a move the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) called “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry”. 




The firm denied this allegation, claiming the workers were dismissed for leaking confidential information. The IWGB insists workers “only communicated in private and legally-protected trade union channels”.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Andy Burnham’s Government Is (Still) Coming for Jury Trials
content:
Palestine and climate protesters who are accused of breaking the law face being tried by magistrates instead of a jury of their peers, according to government plans to speed up the justice system.




Legal experts say the plans to slash access to jury trials will have profound consequences for protest cases, racialised minorities, public participation in the justice system and our fundamental rights.




The Starmer-era Courts and Tribunals Bill will remove defendants’ right to request a jury trial for offences of medium seriousness – known as “either-way” or “each-way” offences. It will also expand magistrates’ powers, reduce rights to appeal and earmark some offences for judge-only trials. 




The bill was introduced in February by then-justice secretary David Lammy as an attempt to deal with severe court backlogs in England and Wales and help victims get justice faster. The backlogs in criminal courts are real, but the bill goes significantly beyond 

Lord Leveson’s  recommendations

 for dealing with the issue. 




And while Andy Burnham’s government claims it has 

“changed course”

 by scrapping one part of the bill, in practice the legislation will still cut access to trial by jury. 




How will the Courts and Tribunals Bill affect jury trials?




All criminal cases in England and Wales start at magistrates’ court. Currently, defendants charged with an either-way offence – such as theft, burglary, drug violations and criminal damage where the value exceeds £5k – can elect for a jury trial at Crown Court. The Courts and Tribunals Bill will remove this right, leaving it up to magistrates to decide whether a case remains in their court for a summary trial where there is no jury, or is sent to Crown Court. 




Magistrates will be empowered to impose longer prison sentences for single either-way offences, increasing the current maximum sentence a magistrate can give from 12 months to two years. 




Moreover, defendants’ automatic right to appeal their conviction or sentence from a magistrates’ court to Crown Court will be removed – instead, they’ll have to ask permission from the Crown Court to appeal. 




The government has scrapped a controversial clause in the bill that would mean offences likely to result in a prison sentence of up to three years were only heard by judges, after justice secretary Alex Norris said he had “heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court”.




However, other clauses restricting jury trials remain, meaning that far fewer defendants will be tried by a jury of their peers – a fundamental right and 

inheritance from the 1215 Magna Carta

. 




Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director 

Tom Southerden described this as Burnham’s administration “astutely judging a concession they can afford to make and get political credit for”, while retaining measures that “add up to very 

significant ongoing threats to jury trial in this country”. 




Tim Crosland, a former government lawyer, previous head of legal for the National Criminal Intelligence Service and co-founder of campaign group Defend Our Juries, agreed, telling Novara Media that Burnham’s government is claiming to be supportive of jury trials while “continuing to undermine them by stealth”. 




“Removing a defendant’s right to trial by jury in either-way cases is a profound constitutional change, which the government is trying to force through without any political mandate, and with minimal parliamentary scrutiny,” Crosland said. 




“Tackling the backlog in the criminal justice system doesn’t explain it. Shifting cases to the magistrates’ court only increases the backlog in the magistrates’ court. It’s robbing Peter to pay Paul.”




Southernden told Novara Media that the “watering down” of appeal rights from magistrates’ courts is “a real problem”, and highlighted 

how the bill risks

 making trials less fair for racialised defendants.   




“Juries have been functioning as quite a significant safety valve for systemic racism in the justice system,” Southernden said. “Members of racialised minorities statistically choose jury trials over magistrates’ trials at 

a much higher rate

 than white people do, because juries are a more reliable source of racially neutral decision-making 

than magistrates are

 for the same offences.




“Juries are one of the few things in the justice system that are found to be not systemically racist in their outcomes.”




Which cases will receive judge-only trials?




Another controversial part of the bill concerns “complex or lengthy” Crown Court cases, which will, if the bill passes in its current form, be dealt with by judge-only trials. 




While complex or lengthy cases are largely presented as fraud and economic crime-related offences, the bill has been 

criticised for failing to include

 any clear definition of – or limitation on – the offences that could be denied a jury trial.




Southernden also warned against the idea that some cases can only be understood by “elites”. “I think it’s important that we reject the notion that juries are incapable of understanding these things,” he said. “If they are, it’s a failing in the law and the way the law is presented.” 




The bill will also allow the secretary of state to add offences to the list of those eligible for a judge-only trial via secondary legislation. There is currently no restriction on the type of offences that can be added. 




A

 House of 

Lords 

committee has slammed

 this proposal as an “inappropriate delegation of power” and a controversial use of “Henry VIII powers” – which enable ministers to amend or repeal legislation with little parliamentary scrutiny.




“The prospect of the secretary of state picking and choosing categories of cases to hand over [to judges only] is hugely problematic,” Southernden added.




The bill has met strong opposition from industry professionals, with the

 Criminal Bar Association

 saying it is “fundamentally opposed to the proposed restrictions on the right to jury trial”. Its own survey of criminal barristers showed around 90% were against the proposals.




These plans were entirely absent from Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, giving weight to the impression that the parts of the bill that limit jury trials target political protest cases. 




How will the Courts and Tribunals Bill impact protest cases?




Crosland believes this is a bill designed to prevent political cases, such as those concerning protest-related offences, going in front of juries. 




“The real driver for these plans is the government’s determination to stop juries reaching the wrong verdicts in political trials,” he said. “It’s deeply embarrassing for powerful people when juries side with those exposing their crimes, whether that’s complicity in climate breakdown or aiding and abetting a genocide. 




“Jury conscience has become a powerful site of democratic resistance to the abuse of power. But if we want to hold on to it, now is the time to organise in defence of it.”




The bill is making its way through parliament at a time when hundreds of peaceful protesters have been 

charged under the Terrorism Act 

for demonstrating against the government’s ban on Palestine Action, and more cases related to anti-genocide direct action are still pending following the sentencing of four activists 

as terrorists after being found guilty of criminal damage

 against arms manufacturer Elbit Systems.




Southernden pointed to how in protest cases “judges are increasingly excluding defences from them and excluding evidence from trials” – 

a key issue in the trial 

of the four Palestine Action activists earlier this year.




“Defendants increasingly err on the side of trying to communicate with a jury about the justice of what they’re being put through,” he said, “and that will be removed from them by the current proposals.” 




The bill has already passed through the House of Commons, and members of the House of Lords began their detailed examination of the legislation on 10 November.

title: Mamdani Abolishes Violent Police Protest Unit
content:
Zohran Mamdani is set to disband a controversial New York City police unit known for using excessive force against protesters.




The New York City mayor laid out plans on Monday to scrap the Strategic Response Group (SRG) in favour of a “civilian-led approach” to policing protest that will put “communication, de-escalation” and “coordination” front and centre.




In a joint statement with the city’s police commissioner, Jessica Tisch, Mamdani said his plan would involve replacing 600 SRG officers with a civilian team and a small specialised police unit to handle protests. 




Abolishing the SRG – a highly militarised police unit that became notorious for its violent and racist policing of Black Lives Matter protests – was one of Mamdani’s core 2025 campaign pledges. 




Under Mamdani’s reforms, the use of tear gas, rifles, painfully loud noises above 90 decibels and kettling – the surrounding and trapping of protesters, usually before mass arrest – will all be banned.




The mayor also endorsed a council bill that would ban the New York Police Department (NYPD) from ever reviving the SRG or its tactics.

title: France Bars Israeli Settler Leader From Entering Country
content:
The head of an organisation representing illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been turned away at the French border.




Yossi Dagan, head of the Samaria Regional Council, was denied entry by French authorities after he landed at a Paris airport last week.




The French foreign ministry said in a statement: “Mr Dagan is subject to an administrative ban from the territory because of his active role in implementing the settlement policy in the West Bank… Settlement activity is contrary to international law.”




Israel declared the move “unacceptable”, while 

Dagan said in a video

 that he was “proud” to be a Zionist, and promised to build “more houses, more communities in Judea and Samaria,” referring to the Israeli state’s official name for the West Bank.




Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967 and more than 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the territory, not including occupied East Jerusalem.




Dagan, an influential figure in Israeli politics, has repeatedly called for the state to formally annex the West Bank, including 

lobbying US lawmakers

 to support official annexation.

author: Charlotte England
title: Home Office Tries to Cancel Online Talk by Pro-Palestine Speakers – Then Denies It
content:
A Green party mayor had to intervene to save an online talk by a leading Swedish climate academic after the Home Office put pressure on the council to cancel the event, documents show. 




The Tribune magazine launch in Hackney, east London, was initially set to include an in-person panel featuring Andreas Malm and Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori, but the panel moved to video link after UK immigration authorities told Malm he would not be allowed to enter the country. 




Organisers have now revealed that in the run-up to the 4 November launch, Shabana Mahmood’s officials appear to have gone a step further and tried to intervene to stop the event entirely.




Documents obtained by Tribune magazine under freedom of information laws show the Home Office repeatedly contacting Hackney council to raise concerns, ask if the venue had been contacted and chase officers for updates.




In an open letter to the home secretary, Hackney mayor Zoe Garbett, who stepped in to save the talk after the venue said it felt forced to cancel, described the intervention as “an appalling assault on free speech” and demanded an explanation.




A Home Office spokesperson said it was “categorically untrue to suggest the Home Office pushed for this event to be cancelled”, telling the Guardian that it had simply provided advice to the council, which ultimately held the power to decide.

author: Steven Methven
title: Cuts to Benefits Are Not the ‘End to Neoliberalism’ We Were Promised
content:
Tomorrow, the government will publish the Milburn report. That’s a long-awaited review into Britain’s one million young people not in employment, education or training – the so-called NEETs. Its contents, though, won’t come as a huge surprise, with its author, Tony Blair-era health secretary Alan Milburn, taking to the Sunday morning news rounds to pitch his plans while others briefed its contents to the press.




They’re trying to get ahead of what could be 

a significant rebellion

 amongst backbench Labour MPs. And who can blame the rebels? After all, with swingeing cuts incoming, they’re the ones who’ll have to explain to young voters with disabilities and other health issues – as well as angry parents – why their lives are apparently worth less than those just a few years older than them.




In politics, life comes at you fast. But not so fast that we can’t remember what prime minister Andy Burnham pledged just four months ago – an 

end to neoliberalism in this country

. That’s a tricky term to define, and while Burnham mentioned deregulation, privatisation and the fantasy of trickle-down economics as its major symptoms, there’s a simpler understanding near at hand. Neoliberalism is when a state decides that corporations, rather than citizens, are its clients.

author: Novara Media
title: Britain Needs an Entirely New Political System. Here’s Why.
content:
Ask anyone in the UK what they think about politics, and they’ll tell you politicians are not to be trusted, and that politics itself is broken. Our institutions, from the Treasury to the House of Lords and the Privy Council, are among the oldest in the world. It is a system better fit for a monarchy, than a modern democracy.




Investigative journalist Adam Ramsay has spent the last decade dissecting the apparatus of the British state. The conclusion he has come to in his new book, Abolish Westminster, is that we do just that. On Downstream this week, he tells Aaron Bastani why and how to do so.




What exactly are the Privy Council, the House of Lords, the Treasury, and who do they serve? Is it normal that so many members of our political system are on the payroll of foreign interests? How have other countries gone about updating their constitutions? And is ending the union the best way to abolish Westminster?

author: Novara Media
title: China’s Green Energy Boom
content:
For decades, the world has run on oil. Then this year, the war on Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz, and a fifth of the world’s oil and gas trade stopped.




The result was a scramble to buy solar panels from China. In March alone it shipped 68 gigawatts abroad, nearly three times all the solar Britain has ever installed.




Its own firms barely make a profit, and now they’re building factories across the Global South. Is this the end of the oil age, and of the American one?




Tim Sahay co-directs the Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab at Johns Hopkins and co-writes The Polycrisis with Kate Mackenzie. He tells Richard Hames how China became the world’s dominant electrostate, why its clean-tech firms are fleeing a price war at home, and what the Belt and Road 2.0 means for the rest of the world.

author: Clare Hymer
title: X Suspends Palestinian-American’s Account After He Launches Senate Bid
content:
A Palestinian-American running for the US Senate has had his campaign account suspended by the social media platform X just days after launching his bid.




Ahmed Moor, a democratic socialist who was born in Gaza, announced on Monday that he would run in the primary to be the Democratic nominee in Pennsylvania in 2028. 




The seat is held by John Fetterman, a pro-Israel Democrat who has voted with Republicans on issues related to Israel rather than with his own party.




On Wednesday, 

Moor said

 that his X campaign account had been suspended. “It’s official! We’re a threat,” he posted on his personal X account.




The account had gained over 33,000 followers within three days of its launch. X has not provided an explanation for its suspension.




Moor, who has criticised US support for Israel and how “wars and tariffs that have driven up costs for working Pennsylvanians”, has said he wants to unseat Fetterman and 

“chart a new path for America”

. 




Fetterman has not yet announced whether he will run again.




“I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing,” Moor said in his campaign announcement. 




“I’m calling for accountability for genocide, for ICE and for corruption. And finally, for the protection of our civil liberties in America.”

author: Sophia Sheera
title: Katy Perry Performs for Tech Firm Founded by Ex-IDF Soldiers
content:
Katy Perry put on a private show for employees from American-Israeli cybersecurity company Wiz in Thailand earlier this month.




Staff at the company were enjoying a five-day luxury getaway in Khao Lak on Saturday, 7 November when the American popstar arrived by surprise, Israeli news outlet 

Israelim reported

.




Wiz was founded in 2020 by “four tech musketeers” who “met in the Israeli army and served together in the IDF for almost a decade”, 

the Times of Israel reports

. All four are graduates of Unit 8200, the Israeli army’s cyber-security arm responsible for the mass surveillance of Palestinians living in apartheid conditions. 




In March 2026, Wiz was acquired by Google parent company Alphabet for $32bn. Google’s links to the Israeli government were already well-established through Project Nimbus, the cloud computing project signed in 2021. 




Perry is yet to comment on the online backlash garnered by her performance. But in May 2024, she shared a Unicef post calling for a ceasefire and condemning the “unconscionable” killing of children in Rafah.

title: Spain Caps Rents and Protects Tenants After Four Million Join Protests
content:
Spain’s parliament has approved a package of reforms aimed at making housing more affordable, a day after four million took part in a 

nationwide general strike

 over the country’s housing crisis.




The measures, proposed by prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s government, include extending eviction protections for vulnerable tenants and restricting speculative property purchases by preventing companies from buying homes for less than 70% of their assessed value.




Rent increases will also be capped at 2%, while those already above the government’s neighbourhood reference index will be frozen. A 10% tax on flats rented to tourists will also be introduced. 




The conservative Popular Party said it will repeal the reforms if it takes power in the 29 November elections, which were called by Sánchez after his government failed to pass similar housing measures.




“Yesterday, the right to housing won on the street and in workplaces, and I hope it will win again at the ballot box,” said interim housing minister Isabel Rodríguez after the vote on Thursday.




Spain has witnessed weeks of housing protests following the eviction and subsequent death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who was forcibly removed from the flat she had lived in for 70 years in September after she couldn’t afford rent increases.

title: Data Centre Decision Taken Off Cardiff Council After Local Backlash
content:
The planning decision on a data centre in Cardiff has been taken away from the city council and will now be decided by the Welsh government, in what local anti-data centre campaigners are hailing as a “massive victory”. 




Welsh planning minister Sian Gwenllian decided the issue was too important to be left to an individual council due to “potential conflict with national policy on transport, energy and flood risk”. 




Developer Curtis Hall is applying to build a 30,000 sqm facility on the site of the Cardiff East Park and Ride, and is seeking permission for gas turbines to temporarily power the site. 




The plans sparked concern over the potential climate and environmental impact  – including air quality, noise, flood risk and water usage – and the loss of the local park and ride service, attracting approximately 3k objections. 




The application has been opposed by all six of the constituency’s Plaid Cymru, Labour, Green and Reform members of the Senedd – including cabinet minister Dafydd Trystan Davies –

 BBC News reported

.

title: ICE-Style Raids Hit Record High in the UK – but Most Result in No Arrests
content:
Immigration enforcement raids in the UK have reached a record high, but most operations result in no arrests.




The Home Office’s immigration team is carrying out more “enforcement visits” than ever before but while these raids leave traumatised people in their wake, the majority haven’t broken any immigration law, the 

Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ) has revealed.




Out of 23,500 Home Office raids conducted in 2025 – an average of more than 60 per day – more than 15,500 (66% or two-thirds) didn’t result in an arrest. 




The figures include raids on homes and businesses, and spot checks in public places like streets, train stations and ports.

title: Is France Prosecuting a Palestinian Refugee on Evidence Extracted by Israeli Torture?
content:
How might a hostile state pursue a refugee beyond its borders? This is a question some fear is at the heart of a case currently inching its way through 

France’s special-track antiterrorist justice system

. 




Four UN special rapporteurs have warned that 2024 charges brought against “Ali O”, a Palestinian national who held refugee status in France, are built on compromised evidence provided by Israel. 




“We are concerned that Ali’s arrest, detention and prosecution appear to be based on information obtained through the use of torture and other forms of abuse against Palestinians by Israeli authorities,” wrote the UN experts, including human rights lawyer Francesca Albanese, in a 28 August communication issued to France and 

published in late October

.




After fleeing Palestine, Ali O settled in France in 2016 and obtained formal recognition as a refugee in 2020. Married to a French citizen and the father of French children, he was arrested at his home in Strasbourg in May 2024. He was subsequently indicted for charges of terrorist financing and conspiracy connected to militant activity in the occupied West Bank in early 2023. 




A memo from the French intelligence services to the country’s refugee administration, and included in the litigation file seen by Novara Media, claims the defendant “participated in the transfer of funds and weapons with military aims” to Palestinian armed groups.




The investigation against Ali O was opened in late 2023. Though French criminal procedure precludes the defence from uncovering certain state evidence, the French state alleges that the defendant was a past member of the Fatah Hawks, a militant group linked to the al-Aqsa Martyrs’ Brigades and affiliated with the Fatah faction of the Palestine Liberation Organisation. It also claims that the defendant conducted online searches on websites used for the dissemination of guerilla tactics and weaponry. 




“[Ali O] committed several crimes incompatible with refugee status. Our service proposes withdrawing refugee status for the concerned party,” wrote the French intelligence bureau. Authorities revoked Ali O’s refugee status in February 2025, even though he has yet to be convicted and is therefore presumed to be innocent.   




Dismissing these accusations, Ali O’s counsel claimed allegations like these would be difficult to construct without close collaboration with outside state sources, notably Israeli. “Ali’s dossier demonstrates the degree to which the French justice system has accepted the role of a subcontractor for Israeli authorities,” attorney Raphaël Kempf told Novara Media, placing his client’s case in the wider crackdown and surveillance of Palestinian nationals residing in Europe. 




Irregularities in the case file also point to Israeli influence in the case against Ali O. The French intelligence memo stipulates he participated from France in militant activity in “Judea and Samaria,” i.e. the Israeli state’s official designation for the West Bank, which is internationally recognised as Palestinian territory, including by France. 




France’s anti-terrorism prosecutorial service (PNAT) declined

 Novara Media’s request for comment. 




Ali O isn’t an unknown quantity for the Israeli state. 




Born in 1990 and raised in the Balata refugee camp on the outskirts of the West Bank city of Nablus, Ali O was 14 years old when he witnessed his younger brother’s killing by an Israeli soldier. Two years later, he was arrested and held in extrajudicial detention before receiving a four-year prison sentence for throwing stones at Israeli occupation forces. It was the first of many stints in jail, according to the biographical information compiled by activists with the Free Ali committee. After his last release from Israeli detention in 2014, he fled to Europe, passing through Italy and Switzerland before making it to France. 




“France recognised [Ali O] as a refugee because of his well-founded fear of persecution by Israeli authorities,” UN special rapporteur on torture Pau Pérez-Sales said at a 29 October press conference following the publication of the co-signed notice to the French government. 




The case against Ali O is based on evidence gathered by Israel from three Palestinian sources. The UN memo warns that one witness, Ali O’s brother, was tortured on several occasions and there are grounds to presume that the other two sources were tortured as well, habitual practices for Palestinians held in Israeli captivity. None of the three were represented by an attorney. 




While the French government is within its right to investigate criminal activities, including cases related to terrorism, “France has an obligation to ensure that its judicial system does not rely on declarations and evidence obtained under torture,” said Pérez-Sales.




Kempf accused the French government of double standards. “The justice system is making the choice to pursue Ali for these charges, just as it is making the choice to not investigate allegations made by my client over the use of torture in the evidence now being used against him,” he said. “By accepting to be the relay for Israel’s accusations against my client, France is de facto validating these types of practices.”




For Kempf, a deeper question remains France’s recourse to terrorism charges in Ali O’s case, pointing to the UN’s recusal of the qualification of terrorism for Palestinian militant activity taking place within an ongoing colonial conflict and occupation. “French prosecutors are operating in a vacuum and are pretending that the outside world just does not exist,” he said. 




A hearing on Ali O’s ongoing pre-trial detention is scheduled for 23 November.

content:

title: Millions of Workers Shut Down Spain With First General Strike in 14 Years
content:
Spanish workers braved stormy weather to go on general strike in protest against the country’s housing crisis on Wednesday.




Unions reported 90% turnouts among dockworkers and carmakers, as millions downed tools three weeks before a snap general election. There were 

“total stoppages”

 at Volkswagen’s factory in Navarre and SEAT’s in Barcelona, organisers said.




Around 85% of meat industry workers, 82% of waste collection employees and 75% from the energy sector are also taking part, they added. In healthcare and ⁠social services roughly 38% are striking while 35% of postal service workers have also joined.




The 24-hour strike, Spain’s first in 14 years, is backed by the country’s two biggest unions, UGT and CCOO, as well as tenants’ associations fighting rising rents and evictions.




“We won’t stop until we transform this country’s housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the rentier minority,” said Alicia del Rio of the Madrid Tenants’ Union.




Mass protest marches were planned for Wednesday afternoon despite the expected arrival of two storms, Charles and Bruna.




Unions pointed to a 10% drop in electricity demand across the country, saying it shows that activity in energy-intensive industries such as steel processing had come to a halt.

title: Workers Building Europe’s Data Centres Face Burns, Rat Infestation and Wage Theft
content:
Workers building data centres for Google, Microsoft and Amazon across Europe have suffered serious injuries, endured degrading living conditions – including rat-infested housing – and been denied wages, 

Investigate Europe has revealed.




One electrical tester was left with electrical burns on 12% of his body after performing an overtime task without safety equipment at a Google data centre site in Belgium. His burns are still so severe he can barely stand being touched, 

he told reporters

. No fines or sanctions are known to have been issued.




At a Microsoft development in Sweden, Romanian workers employed by a subcontractor described overcrowded accommodation infested with rats, broken ventilation and poor heating. 




One diabetic worker had his toe amputated after his feet reportedly lost circulation in the inadequate work boots issued by the contractor, while others contracted tuberculosis.

The ball is now in the Democrats’ court, with the party controlling both the Senate and the House of Representatives from January. But what’s their game plan? Big Thumps – taking aim at risky but headline grabbing knock-outs? Or Top Trumps – smaller, frequent battles for safer wins? 




And can they even play as a team at all?







If there’s one thing that Democrats historically excel at, it’s misreading the public mood. We saw that in 2024, when presidential candidate Kamala Harris failed to harness public anger over Gaza while offering little to allay growing economic distress. She was rightly punished for it. 




Misunderstanding their new position is the most fatal error Democrats could make at this juncture. It must be tempting, high on a win, to see the blue wave as a love bomb from the nation. But when you win big because a 

national majority loathes the president

Now China’s researchers make world-class cancer drugs, cheap surgical robots and cutting edge brain-computer interfaces. Its doctors make AI-powered avatars of themselves to deal with ever more patients.




But China is growing old before it grows rich. Cancer, diabetes, Alzheimer’s and cardiovascular problems are ballooning. And its aging crisis is coming on faster because of the legacy of its one-child policy. How will China adapt?




Ruby Wang worked on the NHS Covid frontline before becoming Head of Health at the British Embassy in Beijing. And now she’s written 

The China Cure: The Rise of Biotech, AI Medicine and a Global Health Superpower

. She tells Richard Hames how China got from barefoot doctors to high-tech hospitals, what it learned from Covid, and what the NHS could learn from China.

Tech justice campaign group 

Foxglove said

content:

The president told voters to

 

pretend he was on the ballot

. They used the opportunity to raise a middle finger to him, Elon Musk – who

 backing Senate candidates that lost – and

 

AI data centres

.




The

 

midterms’ “bluenami”

, along with Lula’s stunning win in Brazil and the

 

student-led movement

 that defeated Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić, represent a wave of progressive victories globally. So why does the landscape at home feel so… grey?

With Andy Burnham now beyond his first 100 days in power, the view from his premiership is looking rather overcast. On Thursday,

in his first speech as PM

precisely because

And frankly, the budget hasn’t had nearly enough hate for being embarrassingly unambitious at a time when people who actually want to live here (not the high-net-worth individuals who are always just about to flee over the mere hint of wealth taxes) are crying out for actual change.




The budget’s £100 sticking-plaster

 

energy bung for households

 in four council tax bands does nothing to solve the long-term cost-of-living crisis or improve British energy security. And this seems to be something of a pattern – big talk and puny delivery. Take the failed monopoly on water: the

 

eight new regional water councils

 announced yesterday will allow local leaders to “set priorities” and “shape billions of pounds of investment” but, crucially, they do not put water back into public ownership.




This is to say nothing of the climate-illiterate decision to green-light new gas drilling in the North Sea, and murmurs that approval of the much more damaging new Rosebank oil field was

 

baked into the budget

.




Alongside the can-kicking and edge-tinkering, there’s also Burnham’s admission in the summer that his government

 

“got it wrong” on Gaza

 and foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s appeal at Labour conference to everyone horrified by the slaughter of Palestinians:

 

“You were right.”

 Both statements are ageing like a tuna sandwich stuffed behind a radiator (if you can afford to turn yours on, of course).




Burnham has

 

rejected Jeremy Corbyn’s call

 for a Chilcot-style public inquiry into Britain’s role in Israel’s genocide, which means the UK public continues to be kept in the dark about the military, economic and diplomatic assistance rendered to a rogue state, in our names and with our tax money, over the past three years.




What’s more, the government has been defending its Starmer-era proscription of direct action group Palestine Action in the supreme court this week, while grannies, the children of Holocaust survivors and a CBE were arrested outside under the Terrorism Act. Why? Because they

 

held paper signs quoting the wife of the PM’s national security adviser

.

Palestine in general

. Burnham’s willingness to keep this authoritarian and antidemocratic farce going is damning, and the footage of retirees being carried away by cops makes Britain a laughing stock on the global stage.




When we can see so much hope elsewhere – from communities united across party lines

 

against sprawling, energy-hungry data centres

 and the anti-human technology they serve, to

 

Brazil’s digital mass mobilisation strategy

 becoming a beacon of global leftist inspiration – the landscape at home can feel frustratingly dreary.




Blame my chronic low dopamine or the leaden November sky for this doomerism, but without strong opposition from Labour’s left, this government will be content to sink back into the centrist torpor of the Starmer years. And we all know how that story plays out – with an emboldened far right and a country run in service of corporate elites, at the expense of everyone else.

title: Google UK Signs ‘Sweetheart Deal’ With Employer-Friendly Union
content:
Google UK has been accused of signing a “sweetheart deal” with an employer-friendly union to undermine workers’ ability to organise within the tech company. 




Google 

signed an access agreement with Prospect union on Monday

 to make inroads among its 7,000 UK workers – excluding DeepMind staff – after 

new rights for unions to access workplaces

 in Britain came into force last week.




However, critics say Prospect lacks a strong record of organising with Google employees – known as Googlers – in the UK. The two largest and most active unions in Google UK are Unite and the Communication Workers’ Union (CWU) via their United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW) branch. 




Prospect was granted access to the Google UK workforce over Unite and the CWU, despite the latter two unions applying for access as soon as formally possible. This means Prospect can now 

communicate with non-unionised workers

 and encourage them to join. 




In a joint Unite and CWU statement to members seen by Novara Media, the two unions warned that Prospect’s agreement with Google is only for “occasional meetings and an internal page, falling far short of the legal minimum requested by your unions”. 




A Google UK software engineer and UTAW rep, speaking to Novara Media on the condition of anonymity due to fear of professional reprisals, called the deal “a huge slap in the face for me and all UTAW and Unite organisers in Google”.  




The software engineer said: “We have worked diligently over the past few years to represent our fellow Googlers’ needs through collective action. We fought to keep as many jobs as possible during redundancies, we demonstrated against Google’s military contracts, and we demanded a stronger, worker-led regulation on Google and DeepMind’s AI direction. 




“For all of our fastidious work, our request for a right as basic as access has been ignored and given to Prospect, a union with laughably low membership in Google which has not participated in a single one of our aforementioned struggles.”




Unite and the CWU are asking why Prospect, which has not engaged in member-led unionising activity at Google, was granted access so quickly and alleging that the Prospect deal was pre-planned because Prospect may be considered a “tamer” or more employer-friendly union.




The Google software engineer added: “This conduct by Google is an insidious way to undermine worker organisation while veiling themselves in the guise of a benevolent, pro-union company. It is telling that this deal was conducted by Google UK’s current senior labour relations consultant, Philip Bickerstaffe, an ex-national officer at Prospect.”




Bickerstaffe worked at Prospect as a national officer from 2004 to 2011, according to his LinkedIn profile, before going on to roles with BT, Boeing, Amazon and Google. 




The Prospect-Google deal follows 

a similar agreement

 between Prospect and Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and Whatsapp. Meta employs roughly 5,000 people in the UK. 




Right of access to workplaces in the UK – even where employers are hostile to trade unions organising onsite – was included in the Employment Rights Act 2025, and came into force on 30 October. 




Unite and the CWU say they put in an access request at the stroke of midnight on 30 October, and received a formal acknowledgement from Google on 3 November, which said their request would be considered and responded to “within the appropriate time frame”.




Employers then have 15 days to respond and a further 25 days to negotiate. The Prospect deal was announced on 2 November, suggesting that little, if any, time was spent negotiating the terms of the deal, which has added to the impression that the deal is favourable to the employer.




Unite, the CWU and Prospect are all members of the Trade Union Congress (TUC), which means they must 

respect the principle

 that a union shouldn’t organise at a workplace where another union already has the majority of workers as members or is actively engaged in significant organising activity. 




Unite and the CWU say Prospect has violated this national cross-union agreement by signing the access deal with Google UK. 




A Prospect spokesperson said: “These allegations are false and seem designed to undermine union organising at Google. Our access agreement with Google was agreed in accordance with the TUC principles and does not include Google DeepMind where other unions are making a recognition bid.” 




A spokesperson from Google UK said: “To comply with new UK workplace legislation, we have established a structured access agreement with Prospect union for Google’s UK employees, but not including Google DeepMind. This step builds on our established work with internal employee representative groups, allowing us to fulfill these new requirements while preserving the respectful, direct dialogue our culture is built on.” 




Unite and the CWU have assured members that they are escalating the matter through the appropriate channels.

title: Palestine Action Protesters Arrested for Quoting Wife of Prime Minister’s Advisor
content:
Twenty-five peaceful protesters were arrested under terror legislation outside the supreme court in London on Wednesday, as the controversial ban on Palestine Action undergoes its final legal challenge on British soil. 




Retirees, health workers, the children of Holocaust survivors, a CBE and a professor held signs quoting the writer Sarah Helm, who posted on X last month, “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” . They swapped the word “authors” for their own descriptor, such as “Jews”, “physiotherapists”, “son of a Holocaust survivor”, “gardeners” or 

“normal people”

. 




Everybody who held these signs was arrested on suspicion of supporting a proscribed terrorist organisation under section 13 of the Terrorism Act. 




Helm is married to the prime minister’s national security advisor, Jonathan Powell. The Metropolitan police 

chose not to take action over her post 

, saying it “did not meet the criminal threshold”.




Many of those outside the court decried this apparent “double standard” in the enforcement of the Palestine Action ban. Officers seemed initially confused about what they should do. Novara Media heard some debating the meaning of the protesters’ placards and whether or not they should make arrests. 




The majority of those protesting outside the supreme court were over the age of 50, as has been the case at all demos against the ban organised by Defend Our Juries (DOJ) over the 15 months of the proscription being in force. 




Actor Alfie Enoch and Massive Attack frontman Robert Del Naja were outside court in support of the protesters. Enoch, who played Dean Thomas in seven Harry Potter films, told Novara Media that the arrests of peaceful protesters happening around him were “chilling and frightening”. He held a sign reading: “This is democracy, not terrorism.” 




Del Naja said he hopes “common sense prevails” at the supreme court, telling Novara Media: “Direct action is not terrorism. These are people acting on conscience to prevent lethal drones destined for the civilian population of Gaza – that to me is a patriotic duty.” 




Among those arrested were Jonathon Porritt CBE, a former advisor to the government, and academic Peter Hallward. Professor Hallward organised a letter delivered to the president of the supreme court, which was signed by 150 leading professors – including dozens of UK law professors – and 1,500 members of the public. It read: “We oppose genocide so we support Palestine Action.”




Porritt, a professor with the Centre for Research in Modern European Philosophy, told Novara Media that preventing genocide is an “absolutely moral obligation and legal duty” and compared defying the ban on Palestine Action to the historic actions of the suffragettes and the abolitionists. 




Trudi Warner, a 71-year-old retired social worker and DOJ co-founder, told Novara Media, that the ban is a “complete mess” and “we’ve managed to show what a mess it is”. “It’s cost the police and the taxpayer millions of pounds to enforce a law that’s obviously ridiculous – it has to stop.”




Warner was arrested for holding a sign that read, “God help us artists who support Palestine and Palestine Action” as she enjoys art in her retirement. 




Tom Southerden, Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director, called the arrests “appalling” and said that people being arrested for using the same language as Sarah Helm “shows how dangerously vague our terrorism laws are”.




A DOJ spokesperson said: “Now we understand what the Met meant when they said Sarah Helm’s message ‘did not meet the criminal threshold’. If you say you support Palestine Action and you’re married to the national security advisor that doesn’t meet the criminal threshold. But if you’re not married to the national security advisor it does.




“Let’s hope the supreme court takes into account the blatantly discriminatory application of this crazy law.”




A Met spokesperson said: “

Officers have arrested a total of 25 people outside the Supreme Court on suspicion of expressing support for a proscribed organisation. The policing operation is ongoing and officers will continue to arrest those who break the law.”




Why is Palestine Action in court?




Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori is challenging whether the UK government’s decision to proscribe the direct action group as a terrorist organisation last summer was lawful. 




It’s Ammori’s last chance to appeal in the UK, and she was granted permission to do so on one ground: whether the proscription of Palestine Action is compatible with Articles 10 (the right to free expression) and 11 (the right to freedom of peaceful assembly) of the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR). 




Ammori has confirmed that if her appeal to the supreme court is unsuccessful, she will take her case to the European Court of Human Rights.




Justices will hear arguments over two days (4 and 5 November). This includes interventions in support of Ammori’s case from writers’ associations PEN International and English PEN, Amnesty International UK and Liberty, a UK Jewish Bloc, and UN special rapporteur Ben Saul. 




The Jewish Bloc, made up of 11 Jewish and Jewish-led groups, seeks to challenge the “fundamental fallacy” that Palestine Action targeted or otherwise posed a threat to the Jewish community, or that it was in any way motivated by antisemitism. It also highlights the particular impact of the proscription of on the Article 10 and Article 11 ECHR rights of the pro-Palestinian Jewish community.




Ammori first took the UK government to court 

in November 2025

, marking the first time a banned group has been able to legally challenge its proscription via judicial review in British history. The high court 

decided in February this year

 that the decision to ban Palestine Action was unlawful because it was incompatible with articles 10 and 11 of the ECHR and that then-home secretary Yvette Cooper breached her own policy in the proscription process. 




The government appealed the high court’s decision, and the court of appeal – the next court up the chain – sided with the government, 

ruling the ban on Palestine Action lawful

 in June.




Since Palestine Action was proscribed, approximately 4,000 people protesting the ban have been arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000, causing 

a record-breaking spike

 in terror-related arrests.

content:

Mao’s biography is a nest of contradictions. He led the largest revolution in world history, then presided over its largest famine – and even then, life expectancy rose 20 years over the course of his rule. He launched rebellions – against a government he already controlled. He purged his enemies and friends alike.




Some 50 years after his death, he remains a central figure in Chinese politics. The Communist Party of China posthumously declared him to be 70% right and 30% wrong, but his face still hangs over Tiananmen Square.

title: Normal People Stars Back Sally Rooney in Letter to UK Government
content:
Hundreds of cultural figures including writers, actors and Nobel literature laureates have signed an open letter in support of Irish novelist Sally Rooney.




The letter, 

published today in the New Statesman

, calls on the UK government to overturn the ban on Palestine Action. Rooney’s support for the group has led to her books being withdrawn from sale in the UK for legal reasons. 




Among the signatories are the stars of the television adaptation of her book Normal People, Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones, as well as the show’s director Lenny Abrahamson.







“Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist,” the letter says. “Her books must be available to the public. Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country. 




“We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity.”




Other high-profile signatories include Nobel literature laureates Anne Carson, JM Coetzee and Annie Ernaux – plus bestselling authors Omar El Akkad, Amitav Ghosh, Jhumpa Lahiri, Michael Rosen, Arundhati Roy and Irvine Welsh.

title: Burnham Approves New North Sea Gas Drilling in ‘Act of Climate Vandalism’
content:
Andy Burnham’s government has given fossil fuel giants Shell and Equinor permission to drill the undeveloped Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.




Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who publicly opposed new drilling before taking on the role, is set to make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning alongside chancellor John Healey. 




In 2022 Fahnbulleh wrote on X: “To have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can’t have any new oil or gas fields. 




“Banks know this, but some are pumping billions into new projects. It’s irresponsible and shortsighted to be funding new fossil fuels when we need to be getting to net zero fast.”
